tells: Measured exposition, gloss of the Arabic term ('reason, ʿaql, the faculty by which we understand, and argue'), Author A's comma before 'and' in a pair, and a closing sentence that leads into the quotation
Picks up the prologue's line explicitly, explains the quotation after giving it, and has the pair-comma habit ('a veil removed, and not a definition learned'; 'Imam Khomeini, and ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi')
'The Qur'an does not describe them as a theory. It describes them as believers.' — a tidy aphoristic closer at the paragraph's end; Author A ends on the substance or on a link to what comes next
'The trouble is being occupied with it.' — clipped, spoken register; Author A would write a full explanatory sentence ('What he objects to is being occupied by wealth')
'What these people see that others miss, Imam ʿAli (as) describes' — fronted-object inversion for effect; Author A opens in plain subject-verb order ('Imam ʿAli (as) describes what these people see')
No trace of Author A's comma-before-'and' in pairs, which shows up in nearly every one of A's paragraphs

Reports the Sheikh by name, glosses karamat/muʿjizat/shirk inline, and keeps the pair-comma habit ('the future, or the past'; 'hear, and see'); the 'Then:' lead-in and the double colon are slightly showier than usual
'Most of us fear Allah's punishment' / 'there is no god but Allah' — Author A writes 'God' in its own narration and keeps 'Allah' for quoted words
'Tawhid is simple to say and hard to grasp' — a neat aphoristic antithesis; Author A explains instead of coining sayings

'Surah Yunus adds to their names, which Sheikh Bahmanpour treats as the same people' — the relative clause hangs off the wrong noun; Author A's syntax is careful ('whom the Sheikh treats as the same people')
'The people of this verse fear Him with a fear that is not about punishment at all.' — a paragraph closer built for effect, not explanation
'The reward. The first gift is nearness.' — a verbless fragment used as a heading inside the prose; Author A always writes full sentences
'in the lecturer's reading' — Author A names him: 'in Sheikh Bahmanpour's reading'
'pure of the filth of this world ... without living in its filth ... concerns that infect everyone else' — heavy, repeated imagery; Author A's diction is plainer ('without being soiled by it')
'and so they understand far better. The second gift is a different kind of life.' — the next point is tacked onto the end of a paragraph; Author A starts a new paragraph for each step

Introduces each authority by name, sets the quotation inside a sentence that paraphrases around it, and follows it through ('It is his own self that he worships'), as A does with Tabatabaʾi and Mutahhari

Picks up 'light' from the previous point, uses a chapter cross-reference ('Chapter Seven returns to that companion'), the pair comma ('through speech, and writing') and A's habit of a semicolon before an appositive ('the path to purity; a striving towards purification')
Reports the Sheikh in plain indirect speech with 'he says', and the short recap ends on the Qur'anic condition without a flourish; the pair comma ('fear, and grief') matches
Opens on a familiar scene the way A's chapter opens on the wedding verse, links back with 'Chapter One argued...', and has the pair comma ('know, and love God'; 'the Prophet ﷺ, and the Imams (as)')
'Each step of this chapter has led here.' — throat-clearing signpost before a recap; Author A moves on to the next point without announcing it
The long closing paragraph goes back over the whole chapter step by step; Author A does not end on summary lines

'ʿIrfan, then, is worth pursuing: it is the training of the soul to perceive and love God, open to every believer, and sought for God alone.' — a tidy 'X, then,' conclusion stacked on a colon; Author A would not cap a paragraph with a thesis line like this
'not because the signs are faint, but because the faculty...has rusted' — a rhetorical antithesis; Author A states the cause directly ('the fault is on our side')
Names Sheikh Bahmanpour, glosses the Arabic, starts a new paragraph for each gift, uses plain diction ('without being soiled by it') and the pair comma ('man, or woman')
